questions.question: What are the four primitives for bounding a self-improvement loop identified by the ICLR 2026 RSI Workshop?
options: Speed limits, memory caps, tool restrictions, and human review
Formal invariants, alignment anchors, multi-objective constraints, and regression detection
Constitutional rules, canary tokens, kill switches, and circuit breakers
Evaluator isolation, sandbox confinement, budget caps, and rollback plans
questions.explanation: The four primitives are: (1) formal invariants checked externally before and after every edit, (2) alignment anchors as immutable core-objective representations, (3) multi-objective constraints requiring all axes to hold, and (4) regression detection that pauses the loop on historical metric drops.

questions.question: What does Lob's theorem imply for self-improving systems?
options: Any self-modifying system can prove its own successors are safe
If a system believes 'I will do X if I prove I should,' it will do X without proving it should—a self-reference failure
Formal proofs of self-improvement require exponential time to verify
Self-improvement loops converge in finite steps under Kolmogorov complexity bounds
questions.explanation: Lob's theorem says: if a system provably believes 'I will do X if I prove I should do X,' it will do X without actually proving it should. This is a well-known self-reference failure that bounds what any system can prove about itself.

questions.question: What is the purpose of regression detection in a bounded self-improvement loop?
options: To detect when the model is overfitting to the training distribution
To pause the loop when per-task score deltas drop below a threshold, catching silent capability loss
To identify when a new self-edit has introduced a security vulnerability
To roll back to a previous model when the improvement stops
questions.explanation: Each cycle's scores are compared against historical distributions. A drop beyond configured tolerance pauses the loop. This catches silent capability loss that would otherwise be absorbed into the running average as the loop 'improved past' it.

questions.question: What is the 'subtle failure mode' of alignment anchors that makes them necessary but not sufficient?
options: Anchors cannot be stored in systems the agent cannot edit
The agent cannot read anchors fast enough during inference
An anchor the loop cannot edit can still be reinterpreted as the loop drifts in how it reads the anchor
Anchors encoded in text can be overridden by in-context instructions
questions.explanation: An alignment anchor prevents editing the objective statement, but it cannot prevent interpretation drift. Constitutional AI is reason-based to handle novel situations, and that reasoning layer is where reinterpretation lives. Anchors are necessary but not sufficient.

questions.question: Why are multiple hard constraints (multi-objective) better than a single scalar score for bounding self-improvement?
options: Multiple constraints are easier to compute than one composite score
A loop optimizing a single scalar will find shortcuts; requiring simultaneous satisfaction of performance, safety, fairness, and robustness axes has fewer shortcuts available
Regulatory requirements mandate at least three distinct metrics for any AI system
A single scalar cannot capture alignment-related properties
questions.explanation: A loop that optimizes a single scalar score will find shortcuts. A loop that must simultaneously satisfy multiple hard constraints (performance, safety, fairness, robustness) has fewer shortcuts available. A modification is accepted only if every constraint holds.

questions.question: What is the honest framing of bounded self-improvement according to the lesson?
options: Bounded loops are provably safe given sufficiently strong invariants
The four primitives are mitigations that raise the cost of silent failure, not formal proofs of safety
Bounded loops eliminate the need for human oversight at deployment time
The primitives together are sufficient to prevent all known RSI failure modes
questions.explanation: Information-theoretic results (Kolmogorov complexity, Lob's theorem) bound what any system can prove about its own successor. The four primitives make silent failure more expensive, not impossible. A bounded loop is safer than an unbounded one, not safe in absolute terms.
